etymology: Aramaic Tattenay (H8674), a Persian name of uncertain meaning, commonly read as gift; the title that follows it, governor on this side the river, is the satrapal office over the province Beyond the River.
biblical_def: Tatnai was the Persian governor of the province Beyond the River in the reign of Darius, and he is the rarest kind of figure in Scripture: an unbelieving official who does his job honestly and thereby serves the purposes of God. When the elders of the Jews resumed building the temple, Tatnai came and asked the obvious question of any provincial governor — Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall? (Ezr 5:3). He did not stop the work. He took down the names, listened to the Jews' answer that Cyrus had decreed it, and wrote to Darius asking that the royal archives be searched (Ezr 5:6). The search found the decree at Achmetha, and Darius not only confirmed it but ordered Tatnai to fund the work out of the king's tribute and supply the sacrifices. Then Tatnai, governor on this side the river… according to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily (Ezr 6:13). Ezra gives the reason the inquiry did not become a stoppage: the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease (Ezr 5:5).
webster_summary: Persian governor of the province Beyond the River under Darius, who questioned the rebuilding of the temple but referred the matter honestly to the king.
webster_full: TATNAI, Aramaic Tattenay, a Persian name, commonly read gift.
Governor on this side the river in the reign of Darius king of Persia.
He questioned the Jews concerning their authority to rebuild the house of God.
He wrote to Darius asking that the decree of Cyrus be searched for in the archives.
When Darius confirmed the decree, he executed it speedily.
scriptures: Ezr 5:3

At the same time came to them Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shetharboznai, and their companions, and said thus unto them, Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall?
Ezr 5:6
The copy of the letter that Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shetharboznai, and his companions the Apharsachites, which were on this side the river, sent unto Darius the king:
Ezr 6:13
Then Tatnai, governor on this side the river, Shetharboznai, and their companions, according to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily.
Ezr 5:5
But the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease, till the matter came to Darius: and then they returned answer by letter concerning this matter.
corruption_summary: Civil authority is cast as either sacred or hostile; Scripture shows an unconverted magistrate doing justice and thereby serving God's ends.
corruption_paragraphs: Christians commonly hold one of two unbalanced views of the magistrate. The first baptises the state, treating political power as the church's natural ally and its favour as evidence of God's blessing. The second treats every civil authority as an enemy in waiting, so that any inquiry from an official is read as persecution beginning. Tatnai fits neither. He was a pagan officer of a pagan empire, he asked a searching question about a Jewish building project, and he asked it properly — through the archives and the courts rather than by force, which is exactly what Rehum and Shimshai had refused to do a chapter earlier.

Scripture's settled doctrine is that the magistrate is God's minister for good, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil (Rom 13:4), whether or not he knows whose servant he is. Cyrus is called the LORD's anointed and the LORD says of him I girded thee, though thou hast not known me (Isa 45:5). The principle to recover is that honest procedure in the hands of an unbeliever is a real mercy from God, worth honouring and worth praying for — for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life (1Ti 2:2).
roots_summary: Aramaic Tattenay (H8674), a Persian personal name; the office is pechah (H6347), a governor of a province.
roots_lines: Aramaic Tattenay (H8674) — Tatnai, governor beyond the river; Ezra 5:3, 5:6, 6:6, 6:13.
Aramaic pechah (H6347) — a governor, a satrap's deputy; the office held by Tatnai and later by Nehemiah in Judah.
Aramaic abar naharah — Beyond the River, the Persian province west of the Euphrates containing Judah.
Hebrew ayin (H5869) — an eye; the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews (Ezr 5:5).
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a minister, a servant; he is the minister of God to thee for good (Rom 13:4).
usage: “Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall?”
“According to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily”.
“But the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews” (Ezr 5:5).

etymology: Aramaic Shethar Boznay (H8370), a Persian name of uncertain meaning; he is always named with Tatnai and their companions the Apharsachites.
biblical_def: Shetharboznai was a Persian officer associated with Tatnai, governor of the province Beyond the River, in the reign of Darius. He never appears alone. Three times the Authorized Version names him in the same breath as his governor — at the inquiry (Tatnai… and Shetharboznai, and their companions, Ezr 5:3), in the letter to Darius (Ezr 5:6), and in the obedient execution of the king's reply (Ezr 6:13). He is a second officer, a co-signatory, one of the companions; and the chief thing Scripture records of him is that when the decree came back from Susa confirming the Jews' right to build, he did what he was told, speedily. The episode is a small study in the sort of opposition that turns out not to be opposition. Ezra 4 had shown the malicious kind, where Rehum and Shimshai wrote a letter designed to stop the work and then made them to cease by force and power. Ezra 5 shows the procedural kind, which asks its question, records the answer, refers upward, and abides by the result. The Jews built straight through the second sort, because the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews (Ezr 5:5).
webster_summary: A Persian officer of the province Beyond the River under Darius, named always with Tatnai the governor in the inquiry into the rebuilding of the temple.
webster_full: SHETHARBOZNAI, Aramaic Shethar Boznay, a Persian name of uncertain signification.
An officer of the province Beyond the River in the reign of Darius.
Named with Tatnai the governor and their companions the Apharsachites.
He joined in questioning the Jews concerning the rebuilding of the house of God.
When Darius confirmed the decree of Cyrus, he executed it speedily with Tatnai.
scriptures: Ezr 5:3

At the same time came to them Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shetharboznai, and their companions, and said thus unto them, Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall?
Ezr 5:6
The copy of the letter that Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shetharboznai, and his companions the Apharsachites, which were on this side the river, sent unto Darius the king:
Ezr 6:13
Then Tatnai, governor on this side the river, Shetharboznai, and their companions, according to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily.
Ezr 4:24
Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem. So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
corruption_summary: Every question put to the church is heard as an attack; Scripture distinguishes lawful inquiry from malicious opposition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Shetharboznai has no modern partisans. The discernment his story requires is nevertheless in short supply. Believers under pressure easily lose the ability to tell the difference between a hostile act and a fair question, and treat both as persecution. Ezra sets the two side by side on purpose. In chapter 4 the work is stopped by a letter written in bad faith, followed by force and power. In chapter 5 the work continues while officials ask who authorised it and write to the king to find out.

Scripture expects the church to be able to answer an inquiry. Be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear (1Pe 3:15), and the elders of the Jews did precisely that — they gave their names, their history, and the decree they were relying on. The principle to recover is that a clear conscience welcomes examination. A work that cannot survive an honest question was never going to survive a real attack, and treating every questioner as an enemy makes enemies of people God has sent to test whether we are telling the truth.
roots_summary: Aramaic Shethar Boznay (H8370), a Persian personal name; associated with the Apharsachites, a class of Persian officials.
roots_lines: Aramaic Shethar Boznay (H8370) — the officer named with Tatnai; Ezra 5:3, 5:6, 6:6, 6:13.
Aramaic Apharsakay (H671) — the Apharsachites, a class or people among the Persian officialdom.
Aramaic kenath (H3675) — a companion, a colleague; the word rendered their companions.
Aramaic taam (H2942) — a decree, a command; the royal word that settled the question.
Hebrew batel (H989) — to cease, to make to cease; the verb of Ezra 4:24.
usage: “Tatnai… and Shetharboznai, and their companions” — the phrase that always carries him.
“His companions the Apharsachites, which were on this side the river”.
“According to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily”.

etymology: Aramaic Shimshay (H8124), sunny or my sun — from shemesh (H8121), the sun.
biblical_def: Shimshai the scribe is the pen behind the first successful stoppage of the LORD's work at Jerusalem. With Rehum the chancellor he wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king (Ezr 4:8), and the letter is preserved in full. It is a model of its kind: no open hostility to God, no mention of religion at all, only loyal concern for the king's revenue. Jerusalem is called the rebellious and the bad city, the archives are invoked, and the conclusion is drawn that if the walls go up the king will lose his tribute. The letter worked. The king replied, and Rehum and Shimshai went up in haste and made the Jews cease by force and power, and then ceased the work of the house of God until the second year of Darius (Ezr 4:24). His name means sunny, which is the irony of the record: a man named for the light did his work with a shadow — not by an edict against the God of Israel, but by a memorandum about taxes, framed so plausibly that a Persian king signed it without knowing what he was stopping.
webster_summary: The Persian scribe who with Rehum the chancellor wrote to Artaxerxes against Jerusalem and caused the rebuilding to cease by force.
webster_full: SHIMSHAI, Aramaic Shimshay, sunny, from shemesh, the sun.
A scribe in the Persian administration of Samaria.
With Rehum the chancellor he wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king.
The letter charged that a rebuilt Jerusalem would withhold the king's tribute.
On the king's reply they went up and made the Jews to cease by force and power.
scriptures: Ezr 4:8
Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king in this sort:
Ezr 4:24
Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem. So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
Ezr 5:5
But the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease, till the matter came to Darius: and then they returned answer by letter concerning this matter.
Ezr 4:7

And in the days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of their companions, unto Artaxerxes king of Persia; and the writing of the letter was written in the Syrian tongue, and interpreted in the Syrian tongue.
corruption_summary: Opposition to the work of God is expected to announce itself; Shimshai shows it arriving as reasonable administrative concern.
corruption_paragraphs: The church habitually prepares for the persecution of the storybooks — edicts, arrests, open contempt for Christ — and is regularly disarmed by the other kind, which speaks the language of good order. Shimshai's letter never mentions the God of Israel. It raises zoning and revenue: this city has a bad history, the walls are going up, the tribute will suffer, let the records be searched. Every claim in it was arguable, the king's interest in it was genuine, and the effect of it was to stop the house of God for some fifteen years.

Scripture warns that the adversary is a strategist rather than a brawler: Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light (2Co 11:14), and the wrestling is against principalities, against powers (Eph 6:12) rather than against the obvious. The principle to recover is discernment about means. Work that is genuinely of God will meet objections that sound administrative, prudent and fiscally responsible, and the test is not whether the objection is polite but whether the effect is to stop what God has commanded. Haggai preached to the generation that had accepted the stoppage as settled, and his word was simply: Consider your ways (Hag 1:5).
roots_summary: Aramaic Shimshay (H8124), from shemesh (H8121), the sun; the office is saphar (H5613), a scribe.

Aramaic batel (H989) — to cease, to make to cease; the whole aim of the letter.
Greek methodeia (G3180) — craft, wiles, scheming; the wiles of the devil (Eph 6:11).

“Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem”.
“They could not cause them to cease” — the later attempt, which failed.

etymology: Hebrew Adoniqam (H140), my Lord has arisen — from adon (H113), lord, master, and qum (H6965), to rise, to stand up.
biblical_def: Adonikam heads one of the lay families of the return from Babylon. Ezra's register numbers his children six hundred sixty and six (Ezr 2:13) and Nehemiah's six hundred threescore and seven (Neh 7:18); and like several houses, a later company came up with Ezra himself — of the last sons of Adonikam, whose names are these, Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, and with them threescore males (Ezr 8:13). The phrase the last sons is worth noticing: the register is careful to mark that these came afterward, the stragglers of the house, and it gives their three names individually rather than lumping them in. The name itself is a resurrection sentence: my Lord has arisen. That such a confession should head a family carried captive to Babylon, whose sons trickled home over two generations, is the shape of the whole restoration. The LORD had said through Jeremiah that after seventy years He would visit them and perform His good word; the return was His rising to do it. The Christian reads the name further still, to the morning when the word was spoken plainly: He is not here: for he is risen, as he said (Mat 28:6).
webster_summary: Head of a lay family of the return from Babylon, whose last sons came up later with Ezra; the name means my Lord has arisen.
webster_full: ADONIKAM, Hebrew Adoniqam, my Lord has arisen.
The head of one of the families that returned from the Babylonian captivity.
Six hundred sixty and six of his children returned with Zerubbabel.
Eliphelet, Jeiel and Shemaiah, the last sons of Adonikam, came up later with Ezra.
Threescore males came up with them.
scriptures: Ezr 2:13
The children of Adonikam, six hundred sixty and six.
Ezr 8:13
And of the last sons of Adonikam, whose names are these, Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, and with them threescore males.
Neh 7:18
The children of Adonikam, six hundred threescore and seven.
Ezr 2:15
The children of Adin, four hundred fifty and four.
corruption_summary: The number six hundred sixty and six is read as an occult signature wherever it appears; here it is a plain count of a family coming home.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 2:13 is a small trap for a certain kind of reader. The number of Adonikam's children is six hundred sixty and six, and the association with Revelation 13:18 is instant and, in this case, entirely groundless. Nehemiah's parallel register gives six hundred sixty and seven for the same house, which by itself should settle the matter: the figures are two counts taken at different times, not a cipher. Scripture uses numbers as numbers far more often than as symbols, and a reader who cannot tell a census total from an apocalyptic sign will find portents everywhere and doctrine nowhere.

The discipline this requires is the ordinary one of reading each text according to its kind. Revelation is a book of signs and says so; Ezra 2 is a register and says so. Rightly dividing the word of truth (2Ti 2:15) includes knowing what sort of writing is in front of you. The principle to recover is sobriety in interpretation: the Bible is not a code to be cracked by the ingenious but a revelation to be received by the humble, and the number of Adonikam's household is the number of Adonikam's household.

“The children of Adonikam, six hundred threescore and seven” — Nehemiah's count.

etymology: Hebrew Hathak (H2047), a Persian name of uncertain meaning, sometimes read as verity or good; he is described as one of the king's chamberlains appointed to attend upon Esther.
biblical_def: Hatach was a chamberlain of Ahasuerus, appointed to wait upon Queen Esther, and he appears in exactly four verses at the hinge of the whole book. Mordecai had put on sackcloth and was crying in the street; Esther, shut in the palace, did not know why. Then called Esther for Hatach… and gave him a commandment to Mordecai, to know what it was, and why it was (Est 4:5). He went out to the street before the king's gate, received from Mordecai the account of Haman's decree and a copy of the writing, and carried it back; then Esther sent him out again, and again he went. He is the thread between the queen inside and the Jew outside at the moment when the survival of the covenant people hung on their being able to speak to one another. Then he vanishes from the record entirely. The book of Esther never once names God, and it is the most pointed book in the canon about His hidden working; Hatach is that argument in miniature. A Persian servant, doing an errand he did not understand, carried the message on which a nation's deliverance turned.
webster_summary: A chamberlain of Ahasuerus appointed to attend Esther, who carried her messages to Mordecai and his to her at the crisis of the book.
webster_full: HATACH, Hebrew Hathak, a Persian name of uncertain signification.
One of the king's chamberlains, whom Ahasuerus had appointed to attend upon Esther.
Esther sent him to Mordecai to learn the cause of his mourning.
He went forth to Mordecai unto the street of the city, before the king's gate.
He brought back to Esther the words of Mordecai and the copy of the decree.
scriptures: Est 4:5
Then called Esther for Hatach, one of the king's chamberlains, whom he had appointed to attend upon her, and gave him a commandment to Mordecai, to know what it was, and why it was.
Est 4:6
So Hatach went forth to Mordecai unto the street of the city, which was before the king's gate.
Est 4:9
And Hatach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai.
Est 4:10
Again Esther spake unto Hatach, and gave him commandment unto Mordecai;
corruption_summary: Providence is confused with coincidence; the book of Esther never names God and is the strongest proof in Scripture that He governs what He does not sign.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the name of God does not occur in Esther, the book is regularly read as a piece of secular court fiction, a nationalist tale that happened to be preserved. The reading mistakes reticence for absence. Every hinge in the story is a coincidence too convenient to be one: a king who cannot sleep and calls for the chronicles on precisely the right night; a gallows built for Mordecai that takes Haman; a Jewish girl already crowned queen before the decree that required her. Mordecai states the doctrine explicitly without using the divine name — who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this? (Est 4:14).

That is providence as the confessions define it: God upholding, directing, disposing and governing all creatures and all their actions, ordinarily through second causes and often invisibly. He does not need to be named to be at work, and the absence of miracles is not the absence of God. The principle to recover is that most of the Christian life is lived in Esther rather than in Exodus — no pillar of fire, no voice from heaven, only ordinary duties done in order, by people like Hatach who carry a message without knowing what hangs on it.

etymology: Hebrew Zeresh (H2238), a Persian name, commonly read as gold or star; the wife of Haman the Agagite.
biblical_def: Zeresh was Haman's wife, and Scripture gives her two speeches that between them frame her husband's ruin. In the first, Haman comes home swollen with honour and choking on the sight of Mordecai refusing to bow; he calls for his friends and for Zeresh, rehearses his glory, and she answers with the counsel that destroys him: Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet (Est 5:14). The advice pleased Haman, and he built the gallows he would hang on. In the second scene, after Haman has been made to lead Mordecai through the street in the king's apparel, he comes home again and tells the same wife everything; and now she speaks the truth: If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him (Est 6:13). She flattered him into the plot and then, with the outcome plain, told him he was finished. Between the two speeches lies the whole distance between counsel that serves a man's pride and counsel that tells him the truth.
webster_summary: Wife of Haman the Agagite, who counselled the building of the gallows for Mordecai and afterward foretold her husband's certain fall.
webster_full: ZERESH, Hebrew Zeresh, a Persian name, commonly read gold or star.
The wife of Haman the Agagite, chief minister of Ahasuerus.
She advised him to build a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai.
The counsel pleased Haman, and he caused the gallows to be made.
After Haman's humiliation she told him he should surely fall before Mordecai.
scriptures: Est 5:10
Nevertheless Haman refrained himself: and when he came home, he sent and called for his friends, and Zeresh his wife.
Est 5:14

Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made.
Est 6:13

And Haman told Zeresh his wife and all his friends every thing that had befallen him. Then said his wise men and Zeresh his wife unto him, If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him.
Est 4:5
Then called Esther for Hatach, one of the king's chamberlains, whom he had appointed to attend upon her, and gave him a commandment to Mordecai, to know what it was, and why it was.
corruption_summary: Counsel is judged by whether it pleases; Scripture judges it by whether it is true, and warns that flattery is a snare.
corruption_paragraphs: Zeresh is a case study in the counsel that agrees. Haman came home in a rage he could not justify, and his wife and friends did not ask him whether a grown man ought to be undone by one Jew who would not bow. They proposed a gallows fifty cubits high — a scaffold so absurdly tall it could only be about display — and they told him to go in merrily to the banquet afterward. And the thing pleased Haman. That clause is the indictment of the whole scene. The advice was measured by his pleasure rather than by the truth, and it built the instrument of his death.

Scripture is blunt about this. A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet (Pro 29:5); faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful (Pro 27:6); and in the multitude of counsellers there is safety (Pro 11:14) assumes counsellors willing to disagree. The principle to recover is that the people around a proud man have a duty to contradict him, and that a household or a church which has learned only to affirm its leader is building him a gallows. Note too where Zeresh ends: she saw the truth clearly enough at the last, and by then the only thing she could offer was a prediction of doom.
roots_summary: Hebrew Zeresh (H2238), a Persian personal name; the wife of Haman the Agagite.
roots_lines: Hebrew Zeresh (H2238) — the wife of Haman; Esther 5:10, 5:14, 6:13.
Hebrew Haman (H2001) — the Agagite, of the seed of Israel's ancient enemy Amalek (1Sa 15:8).
Hebrew ets (H6086) — a tree, wood, a gallows; the fifty-cubit gallows Haman built.
Hebrew chalaq (H2505) — to be smooth, to flatter; a flattering mouth worketh ruin (Pro 26:28).
Hebrew gaon (H1347) — pride, excellency; pride goeth before destruction (Pro 16:18).

“Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high” — and the thing pleased Haman.
“Thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him”.

etymology: Hebrew Arach (H733), wayfaring or traveller — from arach (H732), to journey, to go on the road; the noun orach (H734) is a path or way of life.
biblical_def: Arah is the head of one of the lay families of the return — the children of Arah, seven hundred seventy and five in Ezra's register (Ezr 2:5), six hundred fifty and two in Nehemiah's (Neh 7:10). A second Arah appears in the genealogy of Asher, a son of Ulla (1Ch 7:39). The name means wayfaring, and it belonged to a household whose defining act was a journey: some nine hundred miles from Babylon to Jerusalem, on foot, with children and goods, to a ruined city most of them had never seen. Scripture uses the road as its standing figure for the whole of the believing life. Abraham went out not knowing whither he went; the patriarchs confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth (Heb 11:13); the psalmist prays I am a stranger in the earth: hide not thy commandments from me (Psa 119:19); and the earliest name for the Christian faith in Acts is simply the way (Act 9:2). A family called traveller in the register of the homecoming is the Bible's own picture of the church: a people on the road, whose citizenship is elsewhere and whose settlement is not yet.
webster_summary: Head of a lay family of the return from Babylon; also a son of Ulla in the genealogy of Asher. The name means wayfaring.
webster_full: ARAH, Hebrew Arach, wayfaring, traveller.
1. The head of one of the families that returned from the Babylonian captivity.
Seven hundred seventy and five of his children returned with Zerubbabel.
Nehemiah's register numbers them six hundred fifty and two.
2. A son of Ulla, of the tribe of Asher.
scriptures: Ezr 2:5
The children of Arah, seven hundred seventy and five.
Neh 7:10
The children of Arah, six hundred fifty and two.
And the sons of Ulla; Arah, and Haniel, and Rezia.
Ezr 8:6
Of the sons also of Adin; Ebed the son of Jonathan, and with him fifty males.
corruption_summary: Pilgrimage is turned into a metaphor for an aimless personal journey; Scripture's pilgrim is going somewhere definite on a road already marked.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religious talk is full of journeys. The word has come to mean a private, open-ended process of self-discovery in which the travelling is the point and arrival would be a kind of failure; a man is said to be on a journey precisely when he has stopped believing anything in particular. Scripture's pilgrim language means nearly the opposite. Abraham went out not knowing the route, but he knew the Guide and he knew the destination — he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God (Heb 11:10). The exiles of Ezra 2 were not exploring; they were going home, to a named city, under a decree.

The road itself is marked. Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls (Jer 6:16). Christ does not offer to accompany a man on his own journey; He says I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me (Joh 14:6). The principle to recover is that the Christian life is a pilgrimage rather than a wander — strangers and pilgrims here, certainly, but with a country prepared, a road revealed, and a Forerunner already entered.
roots_summary: Hebrew Arach (H733), from arach (H732), to journey, to travel; the noun orach (H734) is a path.
roots_lines: Hebrew arach (H732) — to journey, to go on the road, to wander as a traveller.
Hebrew Arach (H733) — head of a returning family, Ezra 2:5, Nehemiah 7:10; also an Asherite, 1 Chronicles 7:39.
Hebrew orach (H734) — a path, a way of life; the path of the just is as the shining light (Pro 4:18).
Hebrew ger (H1616) — a sojourner, a stranger dwelling in a land not his own.
Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a pilgrim, a resident foreigner; strangers and pilgrims on the earth (Heb 11:13).

“And the sons of Ulla; Arah, and Haniel, and Rezia”.
“Strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13).

etymology: Hebrew Attay (H6262), timely or opportune — from eth (H6256), a time, a season, the right moment.
biblical_def: Three men in Scripture bear this name, and the first is the most remarkable. Sheshan of Judah had no sons, only daughters, and an Egyptian servant named Jarha; and Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant to wife; and she bare him Attai (1Ch 2:35). So the line of Judah runs on through the son of an Egyptian bondman, married into the family by his master's deliberate act. The second Attai is one of the Gadites who separated themselves to David at the hold in the wilderness — men of might, and men of war fit for the battle, whose faces were like the faces of lions, and Attai stands sixth among them (1Ch 12:11). The third is a son of Rehoboam by Maachah the daughter of Absalom (2Ch 11:20). The name means timely, from eth, the word for the appointed season — to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven (Ecc 3:1). Each of the three men stands at a moment when timing was everything: a line continued, a king reinforced in exile, a dynasty extended.
webster_summary: The name of three men: a descendant of Judah through Jarha the Egyptian, a Gadite captain who joined David, and a son of Rehoboam.
webster_full: ATTAI, Hebrew Attay, timely, opportune; from eth, a season.
1. Son of Jarha the Egyptian servant by the daughter of Sheshan, of the tribe of Judah.
2. One of the Gadites who separated themselves unto David in the wilderness hold.
He was the sixth of those men of might and men of war fit for the battle.
3. A son of Rehoboam by Maachah the daughter of Absalom.
scriptures: And Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant to wife; and she bare him Attai.
Attai the sixth, Eliel the seventh,
And after her he took Maachah the daughter of Absalom; which bare him Abijah, and Attai, and Ziza, and Shelomith.
Ezr 2:5
The children of Arah, seven hundred seventy and five.
corruption_summary: Bloodline is treated as the measure of belonging; the line of Judah runs through the son of an Egyptian servant.
corruption_paragraphs: The genealogies of Chronicles are sometimes read as pure ethnic bookkeeping, a nation proving its purity. They keep undercutting that reading themselves. Sheshan had no son to carry the name, and rather than let the line die he gave his daughter to Jarha, his Egyptian slave — and Attai, the son of that marriage, carries the house of Judah forward. The chronicler records the servant's nationality without apology and without concealment. Israel's registers are full of such joints: Rahab of Jericho, Ruth of Moab, Uriah the Hittite, all standing in the line that ends at Bethlehem.

The doctrine this serves is one the New Testament states outright: they are not all Israel, which are of Israel: neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children (Rom 9:6-7), and conversely if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise (Gal 3:29). Belonging to the covenant people has never finally been a matter of descent; it is a matter of God's election and of faith in the promised Seed. The principle to recover is that the church has no aristocracy of birth, and any congregation that quietly ranks its members by family or heritage has forgotten who Attai's father was.
roots_summary: Hebrew Attay (H6262), from eth (H6256), a time, a season, an appointed moment.
roots_lines: Hebrew eth (H6256) — a time, a season; to every thing there is a season (Ecc 3:1).
Hebrew Attay (H6262) — borne by three men; 1 Chronicles 2:35, 12:11, 2 Chronicles 11:20.
Hebrew Sheshan (H8348) — the man of Judah who had no sons, only daughters (1Ch 2:34).
Hebrew Yarcha (H3398) — Jarha, the Egyptian servant who married his master's daughter.
Greek kairos (G2540) — a season, an opportune time; in due time Christ died for the ungodly (Rom 5:6).

“Attai the sixth, Eliel the seventh” — among the Gadites who came to David.
“Which bare him Abijah, and Attai, and Ziza, and Shelomith”.

etymology: Hebrew Qore (H6981), a crier or partridge — from qara (H7121), to call, to cry out, to proclaim; the partridge is named in Hebrew for its call.
biblical_def: Kore is a name in the Levitical line of Korah, borne by more than one man charged with keeping a door. Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, was with his brethren over the work of the service, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle, and their fathers before them had been keepers of the entry (1Ch 9:19). In David's ordering of the porters, of the Korhites was Meshelemiah the son of Kore (1Ch 26:1), and the divisions of the porters were reckoned among the sons of Kore, and among the sons of Merari (1Ch 26:19). Another Kore, the son of Imnah the Levite, appears under Hezekiah as the porter toward the east… over the freewill offerings of God, to distribute the oblations of the LORD, and the most holy things (2Ch 31:14). The pattern is consistent: this family kept doors and handled what came through them. It is worth remembering whose descendants these were. Korah led the rebellion that the earth swallowed, but the children of Korah died not (Num 26:11), and their sons became doorkeepers of the house of God and the singers of eleven psalms — one of which says I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness (Psa 84:10).
webster_summary: A name in the Levitical house of Korah, borne by keepers of the gates of the sanctuary and by the officer over the freewill offerings under Hezekiah.
webster_full: KORE, Hebrew Qore, a crier, or partridge; from qara, to call.
1. Father of Shallum, keeper of the gates of the tabernacle, of the house of Korah.
2. Father of Meshelemiah, chief of the porters in the divisions appointed by David.
The divisions of the porters were among the sons of Kore and the sons of Merari.
3. Kore the son of Imnah, porter toward the east, over the freewill offerings under Hezekiah.
scriptures: And Shallum the son of Kore, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah, and his brethren, of the house of his father, the Korahites, were over the work of the service, keepers of the gates of the tabernacle: and their fathers, being over the host of the LORD, were keepers of the entry.
Concerning the divisions of the porters: Of the Korhites was Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph.
These are the divisions of the porters among the sons of Kore, and among the sons of Merari.
And Kore the son of Imnah the Levite, the porter toward the east, was over the freewill offerings of God, to distribute the oblations of the LORD, and the most holy things.
corruption_summary: Guarding the door of the church is dismissed as gatekeeping; Scripture makes it an appointed office with the holy things at stake.
corruption_paragraphs: To call someone a gatekeeper is now an accusation — the charge that a person is hoarding access to something that ought to be open to all. Applied to the church the complaint runs that membership standards, confessional subscription, fencing the Lord's table and examining candidates for office are all exclusionary machinery. Israel had an office for exactly this work and treated it as a sacred trust. The sons of Kore were keepers of the gates of the tabernacle by appointment, their fathers keepers of the entry before them, and the reason the post existed was that what lay inside was holy.

The New Testament keeps the duty and raises it. Elders watch for your souls, as they that must give account (Heb 13:17); a man is to examine himself before eating of that bread (1Co 11:28); hands are to be laid suddenly on no man (1Ti 5:22); and the church is charged to put away from among itself the wicked person (1Co 5:13). None of this restricts the gospel, which is preached freely to every creature. It guards the table and the office. The principle to recover is that the door of the house of God is a real door with a real keeper, and that the congregation which will guard nothing will in the end have nothing worth guarding.
roots_summary: Hebrew Qore (H6981), from qara (H7121), to call, to cry, to proclaim.

Hebrew Qore (H6981) — borne by Levites of the house of Korah; 1 Chronicles 9:19, 26:1, 26:19, 2 Chronicles 31:14.
Hebrew shoer (H7778) — a porter, a gatekeeper of the sanctuary.
Hebrew Qorach (H7141) — Korah, whose rebellion the earth swallowed; yet the children of Korah died not (Num 26:11).

etymology: Hebrew Ulam (H198), commonly read their leader or porch — from a root signifying what stands in front.
biblical_def: Two men named Ulam appear in the genealogies of Chronicles. The first is a Manassite, son of Sheresh of the house of Machir and Gilead, whose son was Bedan (1Ch 7:16-17). The second is a Benjamite of the house of Eshek, and of him the chronicler records something he records of almost nobody in these lists: the sons of Ulam were mighty men of valour, archers, and had many sons, and sons' sons, an hundred and fifty (1Ch 8:40). In a chapter of bare names, one household is singled out for two things together — skill in war and a great many descendants. The combination is not accidental in Scripture's way of thinking. The psalm says it directly: As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them (Psa 127:4-5). Ulam's house had both quivers, the literal one and the figurative, and Chronicles counts the second as the greater. A hundred and fifty sons and grandsons, all of Benjamin, is a small army raised in a household over three generations.
webster_summary: The name of two men in the genealogies: a Manassite of the house of Gilead, and a Benjamite whose sons were mighty men of valour and archers.
webster_full: ULAM, Hebrew Ulam, commonly read their leader, or porch.
1. A son of Sheresh, of the house of Machir and Gilead, of the tribe of Manasseh.
His son was Bedan.
2. The firstborn of Eshek, of the tribe of Benjamin.
His sons were mighty men of valour, archers, an hundred and fifty with their sons.
scriptures: And Maachah the wife of Machir bare a son, and she called his name Peresh; and the name of his brother was Sheresh; and his sons were Ulam and Rakem.
And the sons of Ulam; Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh.
And the sons of Eshek his brother were, Ulam his firstborn, Jehush the second, and Eliphelet the third.
These are the divisions of the porters among the sons of Kore, and among the sons of Merari.
corruption_summary: Children are counted as a cost and a limit; Scripture counts them a heritage and an inheritance from the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The prevailing view treats children as an expense to be planned around — each one a subtraction from freedom, income and opportunity, and a large family as evidence of poor judgment. Chronicles thinks the other way, and says so by what it bothers to record. In a chapter of unadorned names, the household of Ulam earns a sentence because it produced a hundred and fifty sons and grandsons who could handle a bow. That is written down as an achievement, alongside valour in battle and in the same breath.

The doctrine is stated plainly elsewhere: Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward (Psa 127:3), and the first commission given to man in an unfallen world was to be fruitful and multiply (Gen 1:28). This is not a promise that every marriage will be fruitful, nor a rebuke to those the LORD has not given children; Scripture is tender with Hannah and with Elisabeth. It is a correction of the accounting. The principle to recover is that a household raising children for God is building something that outlasts every other work a man does, and that the hundred and fifty of Ulam's line are recorded because heaven counts them.
